check.x: Professionalism
Hand hygiene, clear introduction, confirms his name, ensures privacy and explains confidentiality.
Acknowledges the emotional impact of the diagnosis, responds empathetically to his anxiety and stays non-judgemental during the sexual history.
Communicates clearly:

kids.x: Uses plain language, chunks information and explains any jargon straight away.
Checks understanding at intervals (for example teach-back), summarises and invites questions.

check.x: History
Explores what Daniel already knows and has read, and his main worries, before explaining.
Asks about the recent illness and current symptoms:

kids.x: The flu-like illness with sore throat and rash about 2 months ago (likely seroconversion).
Symptoms of a weakened immune system: weight loss, fevers, night sweats, cough, diarrhoea, sore mouth or white patches, headache or visual change.

check.x: Takes a sexual history:

kids.x: When he last had condomless sex with Sam (5 days ago, beyond the 72-hour window for PEP).
Other partners in the last 6 months, condom use and whether they can be contacted.
Previous HIV tests and PrEP use.

check.x: Asks about past history, previous STIs, medicines (including over-the-counter, supplements and recreational drugs), allergies and vaccinations including hepatitis B.
Asks about mood and sleep since the diagnosis, and directly about thoughts of self-harm.
Asks who he has told, his support, his work and alcohol use.
Examination
Asks for observations and weight.
Inspects the mouth for oral candida, oral hairy leukoplakia and ulcers.
Palpates the cervical, axillary and inguinal lymph nodes, and the abdomen for liver and spleen enlargement.
Examines the skin for rash, seborrhoeic dermatitis, Kaposi sarcoma, molluscum or zoster scarring.
Listens to the chest and does a brief neurological screen.
Offers a genital and perianal examination with a chaperone.
Interpretation
Confirmed HIV-1 infection: a reactive screening test confirmed on the supplementary assay.
CD4 count 410: below the usual range but well above 200, so his immune system is largely intact and he does not need Pneumocystis prophylaxis.

Viral load 86,000 copies/mL: a high level of virus, so he is very infectious now; links the flu-like illness 2 months ago and a negative test 14 months ago to recent infection. Viral load is the main marker of treatment response.

Not immune to hepatitis A or B, so needs vaccination; hepatitis C, syphilis, chlamydia and gonorrhoea negative; normal kidney function; HLA-B*5701 negative and no resistance on the genotype, so any recommended first-line regimen can be used.
Management
Explains what HIV does to the immune system:

kids.x: HIV mainly infects CD4 helper T cells, which co-ordinate the immune response, and uses them to make copies of itself.
Without treatment CD4 cells are lost and the immune system fails, leaving the person open to serious infections and cancers.

check.x: Explains that AIDS is the late stage of untreated HIV, not the same as HIV, and is preventable with treatment.
Explains how HIV enters CD4 cells:

kids.x: HIV binds the CD4 receptor and then needs a co-receptor, usually CCR5, to enter the cell.
People homozygous for the CCR5 delta 32 deletion lack CCR5 and are resistant to CCR5-tropic HIV.
The deletion is uncommon (about 1% of Northern Europeans are homozygous) and inherited; his infection shows it does not protect him.

check.x: Explains that ART (antiretroviral therapy) is a combination of antiretroviral drugs, often one tablet once a day, that blocks the virus from making copies of itself at different steps.
Explains the benefits of ART for his own health:

kids.x: Viral load usually becomes undetectable within about 3 to 6 months.
The CD4 count recovers and progression to AIDS is prevented.
Starting early and staying on treatment gives a near-normal life expectancy.
Recommends starting ART soon, whatever the CD4 count.

check.x: Explains that ART is not a cure and is lifelong:

kids.x: HIV persists in long-lived reservoirs (for example resting CD4 cells) that ART cannot remove.
If the tablets are stopped the virus rebounds, usually within weeks, so he must not stop when his tests look good.
An undetectable viral load means the treatment is working, not that the virus has gone.

check.x: Discusses adherence (missed doses risk resistance) and that side effects are usually mild and regimens can be changed.

Explains U=U: once his viral load has been undetectable (below 200 copies/mL) for at least 6 months on ART, there is effectively no risk of sexual transmission; condoms still protect against other STIs.

Until then, advises condoms with Sam, and recommends Sam is tested now and again 6 weeks after their last sex (a test now may be in the window period), and offered PrEP through the sexual health service if he is negative.
Offers support with partner notification for his other partners, including anonymous notification through the clinic's contact tracing service.
Outlines next steps: starting ART with an accredited HIV (s100) prescriber, viral load monitoring, and hepatitis A and B vaccination and the other vaccines recommended for people living with HIV.
Offers psychosocial support (counselling, peer support, community HIV organisations) and discusses confidentiality and disclosure, including at work.
Safety netting

Tells him to seek urgent care (Emergency Department or 000) for fever with cough or breathlessness, severe headache or confusion, a new rash with fever after starting treatment, or persistent diarrhoea, and to call a crisis line such as Lifeline (13 11 14) or come in if he has thoughts of harming himself.

Explains that if a partner has a condomless exposure before he is undetectable (for example a condom breaks), the partner can get PEP from a sexual health clinic or Emergency Department within 72 hours, the sooner the better.
Arranges follow-up within 1 to 2 weeks to start ART and begin vaccinations, gives the clinic's contact details and written information or reliable resources.

desc: This station involves a focused history and examination of a young man who has just been told he has HIV, then interpreting his confirmatory test, CD4 count, viral load and baseline results, and explaining how HIV affects the immune system and enters cells, what antiretroviral therapy can and cannot achieve, and what it means for his partner.
explain:
The virus and the immune system

HIV is a retrovirus that mainly infects CD4 helper T cells, and also macrophages and dendritic cells. CD4 cells co-ordinate the immune response, so their progressive loss in untreated infection leads to immune failure. AIDS is the stage at which the CD4 count falls (typically below 200 cells/microlitre) or an AIDS-defining illness develops, such as Pneumocystis pneumonia or cerebral toxoplasmosis. With effective ART, progression to AIDS is largely preventable.

Interpreting the results

  • Diagnosis: a reactive fourth-generation screening test confirmed on a supplementary assay establishes HIV-1 infection. The flu-like illness with sore throat and rash 2 months ago, after a negative test 14 months ago, fits recent infection (seroconversion).

  • CD4 410 cells/microlitre (22%): below the usual range but well above 200, so his immune system is largely intact and he does not need Pneumocystis prophylaxis.

  • Viral load 86,000 copies/mL: high, as is common in recent infection, so he is very infectious until treatment suppresses it. Viral load is the main marker of treatment response.

  • Baseline tests: he is not immune to hepatitis A or B and should be vaccinated. Hepatitis C, syphilis and the STI swabs are negative. Kidney function, HLA-B*5701 (negative, so abacavir can be used if chosen) and the genotype (no transmitted resistance) guide the choice of regimen. ART generally need not wait for the genotype; here it is already back.

How HIV enters cells

HIV binds the CD4 receptor and then a co-receptor, most commonly CCR5 (CCR5-tropic virus) or CXCR4. This allows fusion with the cell membrane and entry. People homozygous for the CCR5 delta 32 deletion do not express CCR5 on the cell surface and are resistant to CCR5-tropic HIV; about 1% of people of Northern European ancestry are homozygous. This is relevant clinically because maraviroc, a CCR5 antagonist, uses the same pathway, and because it illustrates why the co-receptor matters. It is not something a person with HIV can use or rely on, and it does not explain or alter Daniel's infection.

What ART achieves

ART is lifelong combination therapy, typically an integrase strand transfer inhibitor plus two nucleos(t)ide reverse transcriptase inhibitors, often as a single daily tablet. Current Australian guidelines recommend offering ART to everyone with HIV regardless of CD4 count, and starting soon after diagnosis once baseline investigations are available.

  • Personal health: viral load usually becomes undetectable within 3 to 6 months, the CD4 count recovers, opportunistic infections are prevented and life expectancy is near normal.

  • Prevention: people on ART whose viral load has been below 200 copies/mL for at least 6 months do not sexually transmit HIV (U=U). Condoms are still advised until then and for protection against other STIs. His partner should be tested now and again 6 weeks after their last sex, because a test taken within the window period can miss early infection, and offered PrEP if negative; PEP is for a high-risk exposure within the last 72 hours. Other recent partners should be notified, which the clinic's contact tracing service can do anonymously.

  • Not a cure: HIV integrates into the DNA of long-lived cells and persists in reservoirs, so stopping ART leads to viral rebound within weeks. Treatment is lifelong, and adherence protects against resistance.

Communication and safety netting

Newly diagnosed patients are often overwhelmed. Check what they know, avoid jargon, chunk information, use teach-back, and address stigma, disclosure, confidentiality and mental health early, including a direct question about self-harm. Tell him to seek urgent care for fever with cough or breathlessness, severe headache or confusion, a rash with fever after starting treatment or persistent diarrhoea, and give crisis support details. Arrange review within 1 to 2 weeks to start ART, and make sure his partners know where to get PEP after any exposure before he is undetectable.
focus: Newly diagnosed HIV: explaining the virus and what ART achieves
guide:
In Part 1, the examiner gives findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they would examine. A high-performing candidate builds rapport, takes a focused history that links the recent flu-like illness to seroconversion, takes a respectful sexual history including when he last had sex with Sam, screens for symptoms of immune compromise and asks directly about mood and self-harm, and examines the mouth, nodes and skin. In Part 2 they read the results as confirmed, recent HIV-1 with a largely intact immune system and a high viral load, and note he is not immune to hepatitis B. They explain in plain language that HIV infects CD4 helper T cells, enters by binding CD4 and a co-receptor (usually CCR5), and correctly describe the CCR5 delta 32 deletion as a rare protective variant he does not have. They explain that ART is lifelong combination therapy that suppresses the virus, protects his health and, once undetectable for 6 months, prevents sexual transmission (U=U), but is not a cure. They cover Sam's testing now and after the window period, interim protection, notification of other partners, support, red flags and follow-up.

A borderline candidate may give an accurate but jargon-heavy explanation without checking understanding, omit the co-receptor and CCR5 concept, or state vaguely that ART lowers the virus without covering U=U or lifelong therapy. They may imply that ART cures HIV or that he can stop when undetectable, miss his mood, or forget Sam's testing and interim protection.
patient:
Role: You are Daniel Reyes (he/him), a 27-year-old graphic designer. You are anxious and quiet at the start. If the candidate shows empathy and checks your understanding, you relax and engage. If they use a lot of jargon, say: "I'm a designer, not a scientist. Can you put that more simply?" The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings when the candidate says what they would examine.

Opening line: "I got my results last week and I've been googling all weekend. I don't really understand what HIV actually does to my body. Is this going to turn into AIDS?" If the candidate says they will come back to this after the history and examination, accept it.

Recent illness and symptoms (give only when asked):

  • About 2 months ago you had a week of fever, sore throat, aching and a blotchy rash on your chest. It got better on its own and you did not see a doctor.
  • You feel well now. No weight loss, fevers, night sweats, cough or breathlessness, diarrhoea, sore mouth or white patches in the mouth, headaches, visual changes or new skin problems.

Testing and sexual history (give only when asked):

  • Your last HIV test was about 14 months ago at a GP and was negative. You have never taken PrEP.
  • Your partner Sam is male. You have been together 18 months and live together. Sam has not been tested yet and does not take PrEP.
  • You and Sam have had an open relationship for the past year. In the last 6 months you have had sex with two other men you met through an app. You used condoms with them except once, about 3 months ago. You have contact details for one of them but not the other.
  • You and Sam do not use condoms. The last time you had sex with Sam was 5 days ago. You have not had sex since you got the result.
  • No previous sexually transmitted infections.

Other history: No medical problems or hospital admissions. No regular medicines, supplements or allergies. You had your childhood vaccines but are not sure whether you had the hepatitis B vaccine at school. Alcohol about 10 standard drinks a week, mostly on weekends. No recreational or injecting drugs.

Mood (give only when asked): Since the result you have felt low and have not been sleeping well. If asked directly, you have had no thoughts of harming yourself.

Social history: You have told no one except Sam, who was upset but supportive. You are worried about your family finding out and about people at work knowing.

Ideas, concerns, expectations: You think HIV will turn into AIDS and you will get very sick. You are worried about having passed it to Sam and about your job. You want to understand what the virus does and whether medication can fix it.
points: HIV mainly infects CD4 helper T cells; progressive CD4 loss without treatment leads to immune failure (AIDS).
HIV enters cells via the CD4 receptor plus a co-receptor, usually CCR5; CCR5 delta 32 homozygotes (about 1% of Northern Europeans) are resistant to CCR5-tropic HIV.
ART is lifelong combination antiretroviral therapy that suppresses viral load, protects health and, when undetectable for 6 months, prevents sexual transmission (U=U).
ART is not a cure: HIV persists in reservoirs and rebounds if treatment stops.
Always address partner testing, interim protection (condoms, PrEP or PEP), disclosure and psychosocial support.

stem: You are a GP working in a sexual health clinic. Daniel Reyes, a 27-year-old man, had a sexual health screen here last week. A colleague told him that his HIV test was positive and took further blood tests. He has come back today with questions about what this means and what happens next.
tasks: Take a focused history from Daniel and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining and why (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you Daniel's confirmatory HIV test, CD4 count, viral load and other baseline results. Interpret them, then outline your management approach, including how you would explain HIV and antiretroviral therapy to Daniel and answer his questions, and your safety netting. You do not need to name a specific regimen (5 minutes).
title: Newly Diagnosed HIV: Explaining the Virus and ART

part2.lead: Here are Daniel's results from the tests taken at last week's visits.

handover.label: HIV testing
handover.result: Laboratory comment: second sample tested to confirm the patient's identity, as the National HIV Testing Policy recommends.
handover.model:
• Read: a reactive fourth-generation screen confirmed by a positive HIV-1 Western blot, HIV-2 negative, and reactive again on a second, separately collected sample.
  • For Daniel: confirmed HIV-1 infection, with no doubt about a false positive or a labelling error. With a negative test 14 months ago and a seroconversion-like illness (fever, sore throat, rash) 2 months ago, this is recent infection.
  • What it changes: the diagnosis can be discussed with certainty; he needs ART, and partner notification covers his partners since the last negative test.

rows.t: HIV-1/2 antigen and antibody immunoassay (fourth generation, screening)

rows.v: Positive: antibodies to envelope (gp160, gp120, gp41), core (p24) and polymerase (p66, p51) proteins

rows.n: Second visit (taken when the result was given)

handover.label: CD4 count and viral load
handover.model:
• Read: CD4 410 cells/microlitre (22%), below the usual range but well above 200 (and above 14%), with an inverted CD4:CD8 ratio, typical of HIV. Viral load 86,000 copies/mL (log 4.9) is high.
  • For Daniel: his immune system is largely intact: this is not AIDS, and he does not need Pneumocystis prophylaxis (below 200 or below 14%). The high viral load, usual in recent infection, means he is very infectious now; the flu-like illness 2 months ago and the negative test 14 months ago fit recent infection.
  • What it changes: start ART soon, whatever the CD4 count; condoms with Sam, testing and PrEP for Sam, and PEP after any exposure until he has been undetectable for 6 months. Viral load is the main marker of treatment response (expect undetectable within 3 to 6 months), and the CD4 count shows immune recovery.

handover.label: HIV genotype and HLA-B*5701
handover.model:
• Read: subtype B virus with no transmitted resistance in reverse transcriptase or protease. Integrase was not tested, which is standard when there has been no integrase inhibitor exposure (he has never taken PrEP). HLA-B*5701 negative.
  • For Daniel: any recommended first-line regimen (an integrase inhibitor plus two nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors, often one tablet a day) should work. HLA-B*5701 negative means abacavir can be used if it is chosen; a positive result would rule it out because of the risk of a severe hypersensitivity reaction.
  • What it changes: nothing needs to wait: the s100 prescriber can start ART at the next visit. ART generally need not wait for the genotype, but here it is already back.

rows.t: HIV-1 genotypic resistance test (reverse transcriptase and protease)
rows.v: HIV-1 subtype B. No resistance-associated mutations detected. Predicted susceptible to all nucleoside and non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors and protease inhibitors.

rows.n: not routine at baseline; request if integrase inhibitor resistance is suspected

handover.label: Hepatitis and STI screen
handover.model:
• Read: hepatitis B surface antigen and core antibody negative, surface antibody below 10 mIU/mL (immunity needs 10 or more): never infected and not immune. Hepatitis A not immune. Hepatitis C, syphilis, chlamydia and gonorrhoea (throat, anorectal and urine) negative.
  • For Daniel: no co-infection, so the choice of ART is not constrained by hepatitis B. He is unprotected against hepatitis A and B, both relevant to men who have sex with men.
  • What it changes: hepatitis A and B vaccination (people with HIV may need extra or higher doses and a post-vaccination anti-HBs check), with the other vaccines recommended for people living with HIV. Some tests may still be in their window period after the condomless sex 3 months ago, so the STI screen is repeated in 3 months and regularly after that.

rows.t: Chlamydia trachomatis NAAT: throat swab, anorectal swab, first-pass urine
rows.v: Not detected at all three sites

rows.t: Neisseria gonorrhoeae NAAT: throat swab, anorectal swab, first-pass urine
rows.v: Not detected at all three sites

handover.label: Baseline blood tests
handover.model:
• Read: normal blood count, kidney function (creatinine 84, eGFR above 90), liver tests, cholesterol and glucose, and a normal urinalysis.
  • For Daniel: no organ problem that limits the choice of ART.
  • What it changes: these are the baselines for monitoring on ART (kidney function and urine on tenofovir-containing regimens, liver tests, lipids and glucose); none of them delays starting treatment.

ask: Daniel asks what HIV does to his body, whether it will turn into AIDS, and how the virus gets into cells, because a friend said some people cannot get HIV because of a gene. How would you explain this?
What is your management approach? He asks what the medication does, whether it is a cure, and whether he can stop when his blood tests look good.
He asks: "Can I still pass it to Sam?" What do you advise about Sam and his other partners?
What safety netting and follow-up will you arrange?
